Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. - update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). - schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. That's a complete diagnosis. Here's the full picture.

## What's going on

hyprwhspr's waveform overlay (the "mic-OSD") isn't a normal window. On Wayland, ordinary apps aren't allowed to just paint an always-on-top overlay across your screen — the compositor controls that. The **`wlr-layer-shell`** Wayland protocol is the mechanism that lets a trusted client request a surface on a special layer (background / bottom / top / **overlay**). That's exactly what an OSD needs: a strip anchored to the bottom of the screen, above everything, that doesn't take focus.

**GTK4-Layer-Shell** is a small C library that bridges GTK4 to that protocol. GTK4 by itself doesn't know how to make a layer-shell surface, so hyprwhspr uses this library to turn its GTK4 window into an overlay. Your machine has:

- ✅ GTK4 — works (`Gtk4 OK`)
- ✅ PyGObject / pycairo — works (the Python→GTK bindings)
- ❌ **gtk4-layer-shell — completely missing**

Two things confirm it:
- `ldconfig` finds no `libgtk4-layer-shell.so` anywhere.
- The `Gtk4LayerShell` GObject typelib isn't installed (`Namespace Gtk4LayerShell not available`).

So when hyprwhspr starts, `src/lib/mic_osd/runner.py` runs its support probe (`Gtk4LayerShell.is_supported()`), it throws, and hyprwhspr does exactly what it's designed to do — logs `layer-shell not supported, falling back to notifications` and shows desktop notifications instead of the animated waveform. **The core dictation isn't affected by this** — it's an optional overlay, which is why the requirements file installs it "best-effort."

The fix is to install one system package: `gtk4-layer-shell`. It's not a Python package — you can't `pip install` it — it's a system library + typelib, so it goes through your distro's package manager.

## One thing I need from you first

Your environment variables came back **empty** — `XDG_SESSION_TYPE=`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY=`, `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP=` are all blank. That's because I'm running in a non-graphical shell, *not* inside your Hyprland session, so I can't see them from here. That's fine for installing the package, but it matters for one reason: **layer-shell overlays only work on a wlr-layer-shell compositor** (Hyprland qualifies — it's wlroots-based). As long as you're actually launching hyprwhspr from inside your Hyprland session, you're good. Since your service reached `[READY]` and you're clearly on Hyprland, that's almost certainly the case.

content.text:
Confirmed, and this is the crux of your problem on Ubuntu specifically:

**Ubuntu 24.04 does not package `gtk4`-layer-shell at all.** Its repos only have `gtk-layer-shell` — that's the **GTK3** version (`libgtk-layer-shell0`). hyprwhspr needs the **GTK4** one (`Gtk4LayerShell` typelib + `libgtk4-layer-shell.so`), and there's no apt package for it. So `apt install` cannot solve this — the package literally doesn't exist in your distro. This is the exact situation the requirements file was hinting at when it flagged Ubuntu 24.04.

You have three realistic paths. Here's my honest read of each:

### Option A — Build gtk4-layer-shell from source (the real fix)
This is the only way to get the actual overlay working on Ubuntu 24.04. It's a small, well-behaved Meson project (from Hyprland-adjacent dev wmww). Roughly:

```bash
sudo apt install meson ninja-build libgtk-4-dev libwayland-dev \
     gobject-introspection libgirepository1.0-dev valac git
git clone https://github.com/wmww/gtk4-layer-shell
cd gtk4-layer-shell
meson setup -Dexamples=true -Ddocs=false -Dtests=true build
ninja -C build
sudo ninja -C build install
sudo ldconfig
```

That installs `libgtk4-layer-shell.so` and the `Gtk4LayerShell-1.0` typelib into `/usr/lib`, which is exactly what hyprwhspr's probe looks for. After that, restart the service and the waveform should appear.

The one caveat: your venv was created with `--system-site-packages`, so it can see system typelibs — but only if `GI_TYPELIB_PATH` includes wherever the typelib lands (`/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/girepository-1.0` on Ubuntu, vs Meson's default `/usr/local/lib/.../girepository-1.0`). I'd add `--libdir=lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` to the `meson setup` to be safe. I can handle that detail during the build.

### Option B — Do nothing; keep notification fallback
Dictation already works fully. You just get a desktop notification instead of the animated waveform. Zero risk. If the waveform is a nice-to-have, this is a legitimate choice.

### Option C — Wait / use a PPA
There's no well-maintained PPA I'd trust for this. Not recommended.

---

My recommendation: **Option A.** It's the intended fix and it's a clean source build with no system risk (it only adds one library + typelib). 

Want me to run the build for you? I'll install the build deps, compile with the correct Ubuntu libdir, install, then restart `hyprwhspr.service` and confirm the `layer-shell not supported` line is gone from the logs. Since this uses `sudo` to install system packages and a library, I'll want your go-ahead before touching anything — just confirm and I'll proceed step by step.
